point-01.caption: Placement Before Ukeire
point-01.situation: A South-round decision where the hand is not forced yet, but the current order changes the value of every discard. You may be leading with a cushion, chasing a seat you can reach, or trying to get out of last. The candidate tiles are close enough in efficiency that point thresholds and future danger should break the tie.
point-01.read: Ask what point change matters first, then read the hand. A 1,000-point win that ends a dangerous dealer turn can be excellent from first, while the same win from fourth may do nothing. LuckyJ's top-half games were built on more wins and far fewer deal-ins, so judge the hand by both conversion and loss avoidance. The leader low-risk signal in the data is real but small. Copy it only when the safer tile still leaves the hand a real way forward. If the order needs value, keep riichi, dora, and mangan material before the hand narrows. If the lead is the asset, make the next discard easier instead of chasing an upgrade you do not need.
point-01.whyNot: Pure efficiency gives a clean answer: keep the most ukeire and let the hand decide later. Later can be too late. By one-shanten the hand may already be locked into a 1,000-point result that does not matter, or into a live discard you never had to face.
point-01.copy: When two discards are close, name the point change you need: end the hand cheaply, reach 5,200, threaten mangan, or protect the lead. If the cheap line is enough, take the lower-friction tile. If it is not, keep the tile that makes the hand worth pushing, as long as it does not create immediate danger.
point-01.limit: Do not use this to kill a clearly better shape. If one tile gains a strong tenpai or a much better wait and the safer alternative only feels comfortable, take the real hand unless the score table makes defense mandatory.

point-02.caption: Keep the Anchor
point-02.situation: The hand is still early and undecided: two-shanten or worse, several candidate blocks, and at least one pair, triplet, dora, red five, or yakuhai that could define the hand later. No opponent has forced a fold yet, so the question is not pure ukeire. You are deciding which pieces still deserve time.
point-02.read: A useful early anchor does more than form a pair. It lets the hand become open, valuable, or defensible without a perfect run of draws. Pair and triplet anchors matter most because they can become yakuhai calls, toitoi pressure, a chiitoi fallback, or the stable pair of an ordinary hand. Dora and red-five material deserve the same treatment when they make the final hand worth pushing. The tile has to have a concrete second job. Keeping it because it feels important is not enough.
point-02.whyNot: The pure-efficiency discard makes the hand look like a normal five-block riichi hand right away. Many early hands are not normal yet, and forcing them to be can erase the best value or the open option before you know which draw is coming.
point-02.copy: When the hand is early and messy, mark the tiles that provide yaku, dora value, call permission, or an emergency stop. If one of those tiles also supports the shape, keep it and cut the weak block that needs the most exact help.
point-02.limit: Do not protect anchors after their job expires. If the hand has a fast good-shape path, or the kept tile is a dead honor, an isolated terminal, or a pair that cannot become yaku, value, or safety, take the efficient discard.

point-03.caption: Open With a Reason
point-03.situation: A clumsy hand with one or two bad blocks, a possible yakuhai or tanyao, and an early call opportunity. The offered tile helps, but taking it removes riichi, ura, and menzen tsumo from the hand. The table has not forced you to defend yet, so this is a construction decision, not an emergency.
point-03.read: A call is strongest when it changes what the hand is allowed to do. A yakuhai pon makes the hand legal. A chi into tenpai changes the clock. A call that denies the dealer a draw can be right even for a small hand. The normal open tanyao or yakuhai hand is worth 1,000 to 3,900, so the tempo has to be real to cover the lost closed premium. LuckyJ's record is active and selective at the same time: about 36% of hands involved calls, and roughly 2,000 engine-preferred calls were passed. Copy the selection, not the surface activity. If the call only improves shape and leaves no yaku, no tenpai plan, and no safe reserve, it has not earned the exposure.
point-03.whyNot: Closed-hand thinking says pass, because riichi, ura, and menzen tsumo are worth a lot. That is true when the hand can actually reach them. With two weak blocks, the closed 3,900 is often a story you tell yourself while an opponent wins a cheap hand first.
point-03.copy: Check yaku, distance, value, and the next safe tile. If the call creates a legal hand, immediate tenpai, a strong one-shanten, or a specific tempo gain, take it and discard the tile that keeps the hand coherent. If none of those is true, stay closed and let the table give you more information.
point-03.limit: This does not justify opening every bad shape. Good closed value, a live riichi path, an All Last score that demands a bigger hand, or an open hand with no defensive exit all argue for passing.

point-04.caption: Open, Keep Brakes
point-04.situation: You have already called, or you are considering a call that will shorten the hand. The hand may be yakuhai, tanyao, honitsu, or a keiten chase, and it is not guaranteed to win soon. One or more honors, genbutsu, or suji tiles are competing with ordinary shape tiles.
point-04.read: Open hands need defensive planning because they have fewer tiles to choose from. A closed hand can sometimes draw into safety while staying flexible. An open hand usually has to defend with what it kept before the threat appeared. That is why a 1,000-point open hand still two-shanten should not casually spend its only genbutsu, while a 3,900 tenpai can justify more commitment. A saved genbutsu buys one turn, not a permanent fold. Once it is spent, the next draw decides whether mawashi still exists. A new genbutsu or a low-danger discard that keeps the one-shanten keeps the hand alive. An improvement to a good tenpai can justify a fresh push. If only a live tile keeps the shape, the choice has become a plain push or a fold that breaks the hand. When LuckyJ is fourth against a third-place dealer's riichi, winning gains defensive value because it ends the dealer turn and stops the gap from widening. Dealing directly into that dealer is also the worst transfer, so wanting to stop them does not authorize a chain of unsafe discards.
point-04.whyNot: Efficiency says cut the safe honor and keep the extra acceptance. That feels clean because the hand is open and therefore supposedly attacking. It ignores the future cost: after another call, you may be choosing between folding with no tiles and dealing a live middle tile for a cheap hand. The opposite mistake is treating fourth place as permission to push forever. Stopping the dealer matters only while your own winning route is credible enough to compete with the direct deal-in cost.
point-04.copy: Before calling, check distance and the remaining safe tile. After calling, check again: safe against whom, and on which danger turn? Treat the last genbutsu as a one-turn option. After spending it, start the count from zero. Continue by mawashi if the new discard is low-friction and keeps the strong one-shanten. Push if the draw creates a hand whose value and placement effect pay for the danger. Break the hand when keeping it requires several live tiles. Being fourth against the third-place dealer adds value to winning the hand, not to surviving one risky discard.
point-04.limit: Do not freeze the hand around a stale safe tile, and do not call every no-genbutsu continuation mawashi. Once no tolerable discard keeps the shape, mawashi has ended. If the hand is cheap, the wall is short, or more unsafe discards remain after this one, fold even from fourth. Spend safety more freely only when the hand has enough value, immediacy, or placement need to justify the whole remaining path.

point-05.caption: Trim Future Danger
point-05.situation: The hand is far from tenpai, usually two-shanten or worse, with one or two loose middle tiles outside the main value plan. Nobody has declared yet, but rivers are developing and your own earlier discards are starting to make some later releases awkward. The choice is between a little present ukeire and a cleaner future push-fold path.
point-05.read: A floater is not harmless just because nobody has riichi yet. If the hand is slow, there is a real chance that danger arrives before your tenpai does. An isolated [[4p]], [[5s]], or [[6m]] then has to be judged by its future release price, not only by how many tiles it accepts today. The idea is strongest when the tile is outside your yaku, outside your dora plan, and not part of the best five blocks. This is not an early fold. It removes the tile that would make a later push irrational.
point-05.whyNot: Efficiency keeps the central floater because it sees more tiles than a terminal or honor. In a fast hand that is right. In a slow hand it ignores the chance that the hand has to survive a riichi before those acceptances matter.
point-05.copy: When you are far away, name the value plan first, then find the leftover tile least connected to it. If that tile is a live middle tile that will be hard to release later, cut it while the table is still cheap.
point-05.limit: Do not turn this into a reflex against middle tiles. Keep the floater when it is red, dora-connected, the only good-shape upgrade, or required for the score you need.

point-06.caption: Seed Value Early
point-06.situation: An early hand where the fastest version looks cheap, but you still have flexible value material: red fives, dora-adjacent tiles, yakuhai pairs, or pair-heavy structure. The table is not forcing defense yet. The choice is between keeping a value seed and cleaning the hand for the best immediate shape.
point-06.read: Value is easiest to keep while the hand is wide. If the likely efficient hand is 1,000 or 2,000 and the hanchan asks for 5,200 or mangan, the efficient line is already failing. LuckyJ's supported habit is specific: keep red and dora material that still connects to tanyao, riichi, yakuhai, or a real pair structure. That is different from buying random risk from behind. A value tile earns its place by making the final hand worth pushing, not by looking expensive on its own. When the value plan stops improving the actual hand, it has become clutter.
point-06.whyNot: The efficiency cut often makes the hand cleaner right away, and it avoids holding an honor or dora too long. If that cleanliness produces a cheap, bad-shape tenpai you cannot push, the early speed bought nothing.
point-06.copy: When the cheap line is not enough, keep value material that is connected, pair-based, or naturally callable, and spend terminals and redundant floaters first. Recheck every draw. If the value tile starts costing real ukeire or real safety, release it. Treat red fives and dora shapes as part of the hand, not as souvenirs.
point-06.limit: This is not a license for broad risk-taking because you are behind. Against live threats, or when the value tile is isolated and the hand stays small, choose shape or safety instead.

point-08.caption: Riichi Taxes Everyone
point-08.situation: A closed tenpai or near-tenpai where you can be the first to present a real threat. Opponents have not yet shown enough force to make the hand a pure defense problem. The choice is between declaring now, staying dama, and waiting for a better upgrade.
point-08.read: Riichi turns pressure into points. It adds a han, creates ura upside, and makes every opponent price their next discard under threat. LuckyJ's winning-half games used more riichi, and the sampled pressure riichi get unusually broad outside support. Mortal usually agrees with declaring in them, but declaration support does not show that LuckyJ's discard or wait was best. The question is not reach volume. It is whether the declaration changes the table. Reach when the lock buys value, fold equity, or a placement swing you need.
point-08.whyNot: The conservative mistake is waiting for the perfect wait after the hand is already strong enough. The reckless mistake is reaching every closed tenpai because riichi is usually good. Both ignore the table: timing, opponent progress, and whether the value actually forces a reaction.
point-08.copy: If you are first to credible pressure, the wait is live, and the riichi turns a small hand into a real threat, declare. If the hand is already enough as dama, or the riichi only locks you into future danger, stay quiet. In review, check not only whether the riichi won but whether it changed opponents' discards.
point-08.limit: Avoid it against multiple active threats with a low-value bad wait, and in endgame score situations where dama wins the seat you need. Riichi should tax the table, not donate a stick.

point-09.caption: Reprice Every Draw
point-09.situation: You have a playable hand, but the table changes while you are still short of winning: a riichi appears, an open hand adds pressure, or your draw creates a worse next discard. The tempting line is to keep following last turn's plan. This point applies whenever the hand may need more than one unsafe discard before it can win.
point-09.read: Push-fold is a sequence, not a single-tile quiz. The first discard may be acceptable on its own, and the next draw can still turn the continuation into a bad contract. The nondealer Tokujou sample removes every LuckyJ dealer state and every locked discard after LuckyJ's own riichi. It leaves 46 chosen discards at 90% or more on the maximum NAGA danger proxy. All 46 faced at least one riichi, 33 were tenpai, 12 were one-shanten, 20 were open hands, and at least two NAGA heads supported 30 of them. The repeated 99.99% reading behaves like a capped alarm, not a literal deal-in probability. The supported cases cluster in valuable tenpai, meaningful riichi declarations, and shortened open hands with almost no inventory. The rejected cases show why the alarm still matters.
point-09.whyNot: Efficiency wants to preserve ukeire and decides once that the hand is an attack. That misses the bill for the discards still to come, and it mistakes tenpai for permission. In the clearest rejected case, LuckyJ protected a late open tenpai while leading with 41,000, chose a 99.99% proxy tile over a 2.97% alternative that all three heads preferred, and dealt into a 12,000-point hand. Keeping tenpai explained the move. It did not justify it.
point-09.copy: Count value and distance first, then count the unsafe discards the hand probably still owes. Classify an extreme push before copying it: value-backed tenpai, placement urgency, a pressure riichi, or an inventory trap caused by calls. If the hand is not tenpai or its value is ordinary, keep a safe exit or move through mawashi instead of paying the whole bill. When a new threat appears, redo the count from zero.
point-09.limit: These counts describe nondealer decisions only; do not mix dealer-continuation value into them. Outcomes were mixed, with 12 self-wins, 11 direct deal-ins, 14 wins by another player, and nine draws, so a later win does not show the push was sound. A strong tenpai or an All Last score requirement can still demand danger, but the value has to be explainable before the result is known.

point-10.caption: Count The Last Row
point-10.situation: The hand has reached the third row with long rivers, at least one live threat, and only a few draws left. You may be tenpai, one-shanten, or barely able to make keiten. Shape language is no longer enough. The decision has to be tied to points and safety.
point-10.read: Late decisions are arithmetic. Count the direct win first: value, wait quality, and whether the win changes placement. Then count draw tenpai: whether you can reach or keep tenpai through genbutsu, suji, kabe-supported, or otherwise low-friction tiles. Then count the fold: how many safe tiles you have and whether folding now protects the same placement better than a thin push. LuckyJ's disagreement rate with NAGA drops to about 28% in the late row, which is a reminder that there is less room for style here. The closer the wall gets to zero, the more every discard has to answer an exact point question.
point-10.whyNot: The tempting mistake is to keep using early-hand language: maybe value, maybe shape, maybe one more draw. In the third row, maybe is expensive. A tile that was flexible on turn five may now be a dangerous discard with no time left to cash its upside.
point-10.copy: With few draws left, write the decision in order: win value, tenpai-payment value, number of safe discards, and next-turn danger. If a discard advances one of those goals without creating a worse next discard, take it. Otherwise fold.
point-10.limit: Do not chase keiten through multiple live threats with an unprotected center tile. Do not overfold a high-value real tenpai just because the row is late, either. If the hand is worth pushing and the discard is tolerable, attack.

point-11.caption: Keiten Is Value
point-11.situation: A late hand with few tiles left where an outright win has become unlikely but tenpai is still reachable. One or more opponents may be threatening, and the candidate discards differ mainly in safety and in whether they keep a final tenpai shape. The decision is safe tenpai versus clean noten, not attack versus fold.
point-11.read: Noten payments are part of the hand's value. A 1,000 to 3,000 swing can protect first, pull you out of last, or force someone else to chase in the next hand. LuckyJ was tenpai in 823 of 1,761 exhaustive draws (46.7%, or 6.3% of all 13,054 hands). That is often enough to study rather than improvise. The right keiten chase uses genbutsu, dead tiles, kabe-supported tiles, or tiles the threat has already accepted. The wrong chase asks a dangerous tile to survive because the wall is short. Count both the payment and the danger of each tile needed to reach it.
point-11.whyNot: Pure defense is tempting because noten feels cheaper than a deal-in, and it often is. Pure attack is tempting because tenpai payments are visible and immediate. Both go wrong when they ignore the exact discard path. Safe tenpai is valuable. Unsafe keiten is not.
point-11.copy: With the wall short, count how many safe or nearly safe discards get you to tenpai. If the answer is one or two harmless tiles, keep the shape and take the draw value. If the answer includes a live middle tile against a real threat, fold first and let the payment go.
point-11.limit: This does not apply when the hand still has a strong winning chance worth pushing normally. Evaluate that as an attack. It also does not apply when tenpai requires danger that exceeds the 1,000 to 3,000 reward.

point-12.caption: Splits Are Homework
point-12.situation: You are reviewing a hand where LuckyJ, Nishiki, the other NAGA heads, or Mortal disagree on the best discard. The move may be early and quiet, or a real push-fold decision with points at stake. The risk is treating one model's answer as a command instead of a question.
point-12.read: The book's method is conditional copying. LuckyJ's top-discard match with NAGA is about 73%, high enough to respect the engine and low enough to make the mismatches worth studying. Over 36,000 LuckyJ/Nishiki mismatches give plenty of material, and a mismatch alone does not say who is right. The NAGA heads disagree among themselves, and Mortal often backs Nishiki or picks a third line in this review set. That is useful, because it forces you to separate blunders from style trade-offs and real insights. Copy the move only when you can state what it buys in points, safety, speed, pressure, or placement.
point-12.whyNot: It is easy to defer to the highest engine line because it feels objective. It is just as easy to defer to LuckyJ because the project is about LuckyJ. Neither shortcut teaches you why a -3,900 risk is unacceptable in one hand and a +2,900 purchase is worth keeping in another.
point-12.copy: For every split, write three short claims before looking at the result: what LuckyJ bought, what the engine bought, and what each line risked. If LuckyJ's purchase is clear and repeatable, test it against score, danger, and hand value, then add it to your playbook. If you cannot explain it, file it as uncertain instead of imitating it.
point-12.limit: Do not use engine disagreement to excuse fundamentals. Missed yaku, furiten, obvious betaori spots, and noten late pushes are still mistakes even when one model split makes them look sophisticated.

point-13.caption: Price the Missing Yakuhai
point-13.situation: An opponent has opened, but their yaku is not visible yet. The exposed tiles could still be tanyao, honitsu, yakuhai, chanta, or plain atozuke. You hold a loose dragon, the round wind, or that opponent's seat wind, and your own hand is not ready to punish them.
point-13.read: The live yakuhai may be the opponent's missing permission to win, so carrying it and discarding it both have a price. Discarding it offers the pon. It is not denial. The deliberate early line releases the tile while no yaku and no clear advancement are visible, accepting today's pon risk so the tile is not carried into a more dangerous visible context. The later line chokes it once calls, turn, or river make advancement plausible. The observed cut medians describe timing only. The sample is conditioned on the tile surviving until each open-hand context, so it does not show that an opponent's call caused LuckyJ to wait, or how far the concealed hand was.
point-13.whyNot: Keeping the honor preserves the option of choking the open hand, and it can also become a dangerous live tile that blocks your own route. Releasing it preserves shape and may hand the opponent an immediate yaku. Price those two costs directly instead of calling either action automatic defense.
point-13.copy: After every unclear call, mark dragons, the round wind, and that player's seat wind as possible yaku switches. Release a singleton only while no yaku or clear advancement is visible. Once advancement is visible, choke it unless your own value, safety, or placement makes feeding acceptable.
point-13.limit: The selected examples are engine-contested. Treat the move as a stress test, not a default, and keep the tile when it is your pair, your yaku, your only safe tile, or part of a concrete value plan.

point-14.caption: Safety Has a Target
point-14.situation: You are choosing between trimming shape and spending a tile that is genbutsu, suji, or otherwise safer against one opponent. There is a real or credible threat on the table: a riichi, dealer pressure, a fast open hand, or a river that will soon force betaori. The question is whether the defensive tile answers that exact player.
point-14.read: Genbutsu is the strongest answer because it is a same-tile answer to one opponent's river. Suji is weaker but still practical when it points at the player you may have to fold against. LuckyJ's results fit this habit: about 13,000 hands, a 22.9% win rate, and a 10.1% deal-in rate. The placement split is sharper, with 0.75 deal-ins per game in top-half games against 1.48 in bottom-half games. The lesson is not to keep every safe-looking tile. It is to keep the one that turns a future forced live discard into a controlled fold or a mawashi turn. A tile that avoids one -4,000 loss is worth more than a small amount of shape.
point-14.whyNot: Efficiency dislikes defensive clutter because the table may stay quiet. That objection is right when the tile has no opponent attached. It is wrong when spending the tile leaves your next bad draw with no answer to the dealer, the riichi player, or the open hand already applying pressure.
point-14.copy: Name the player first, then the event: riichi, second call, bad draw, or late keiten fight. If the tile is genbutsu or solid suji against that player and your hand is not strong enough to ignore danger, keep it over a marginal shape tile. Recheck the label whenever the main threat changes.
point-14.limit: Do not overrate generic safety. Weak suji, old outside tiles, and genbutsu against a quiet opponent should not block a good hand unless they also defend against the player likely to attack next.

point-15.caption: Stale Safety Costs Shape
point-15.situation: You hold a tile that was safe against someone earlier, but the table has moved on. Another opponent has riichi, the open hand is now the pressure, or your own hand is close enough that the old safe tile blocks the clean tenpai line. NAGA may prefer keeping the comfort tile while LuckyJ spends it.
point-15.read: Safe tiles expire. The previous chapter says to keep safety for a specific opponent. This one says to spend it when that opponent is no longer the problem. LuckyJ's more than 4,000 stale-safety spends were not reckless attacks, because each came with a current-danger check. The same data supports more than 8,400 threat-specific keeps, so the rule cuts both ways: keep live safety, spend dead safety. A +2,300 hand is a real purchase. Letting it decay into a -1,500 draw because you protected against the wrong player is not careful play. Careful play is knowing which safety still has value.
point-15.whyNot: Keeping a safe-looking tile feels disciplined. Often it is only fear with a label. If the tile does not answer the live riichi or the player most likely to win, holding it damages your shape and can make your next good draw unusable.
point-15.copy: Identify the current danger first, then compare your safe tiles against that player. If the old tile protects a quiet opponent, you have another real safe tile, and the hand is close enough to care about shape, discard the stale tile. If those conditions are not met, keep the brake.
point-15.limit: Do not spend stale-looking safety in thin late hands with no second safe tile. Do not spend it when the original opponent is still the main threat, or when betaori is already the best result.

point-16.caption: Attack Through Edges
point-16.situation: The hand is usually in the middle or late rows, close enough that keeping tenpai shape matters, and the table has enough danger that a lower-friction discard has value. The choice is between an outside tile, often [[1m]], [[9p]], or a side tile, and a middle tile that keeps the hand connected. You have to decide whether the outside cut only looks safe or actually protects the winning shape.
point-16.read: A terminal discard can be an attacking discard when it buys the right to keep the center. Middle tiles connect three-away shapes: [[3p]][[4p]] wants [[2p]] or [[5p]], [[6p]][[7p]] wants [[5p]] or [[8p]], and the tile between them often keeps both alive. If the outside tile does not support value, yaku, pair structure, or real safety, it is weaker than it looks. That is why LuckyJ often spends the edge and keeps the inner line. The hand is choosing the discard that keeps the best win path with the least immediate exposure, not giving up.
point-16.whyNot: Terminals feel safe and middle tiles feel dangerous, so the reflex is to cut the middle tile. That reflex ignores shape. If the middle tile is the bridge to a good tenpai, cutting it turns a real hand into a pile of safer leftovers.
point-16.copy: When an outside cut looks strange, look at the tile you keep. If the kept middle tile forms a ryanmen, repairs a bad block, keeps a perfect one-shanten, or avoids a worse live discard next turn, the edge cut is usually the practical attack.
point-16.limit: This does not apply when the outside tile has a stronger job than the center. Dora terminals, chiitoi pairs, honitsu or chanta material, and exact genbutsu against the main threat have to be priced before you call the middle tile essential.

point-18.caption: Label the Honor
point-18.situation: Your hand holds one or more honors while the table is still changing. Some may be your own yakuhai, some may be useful to an open opponent, and some may be nothing but defensive material. A pure efficiency discard and an honor discard both look plausible.
point-18.read: Give the honor a role first, because different roles produce opposite discards. Self-value honors stay when they create yaku, pair value, honitsu, chiitoi, or dora scaling. Opponent-condition honors go early when an unclear open hand could use them as its legal yaku. Dead honors and genbutsu honors are defensive material, but only against the threats they actually answer. LuckyJ's turn split shows the difference: some lone yakuhai are gone around turn 3, while similar-looking honors in open-hand contexts can wait until around turn 9. Strong honor play is role-first, not yakuhai-first or yakuhai-last.
point-18.whyNot: The easy habit is one slogan: cut honors early, keep honors for safety, or hold yakuhai pairs forever. Each slogan wins some hands and ruins others. Without the role label you cannot tell whether the tile is earning value for you, handing legality to someone else, or buying a future fold.
point-18.copy: For each honor, ask four questions in order: is it my yaku or value, is it someone else's missing yaku, is it dead, and is it safe against the real threat? If one answer is clearly strongest, play that role. If two roles conflict, use score and distance. A slow hand from behind values self yaku more. A lead against riichi values defense more.
point-18.limit: Do not keep a label out of habit. Recheck after every call, riichi, second visible copy, and late abnormal river. Honors change status faster than suit tiles, because one pon can change both legality and danger.
